title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Coldwater officials hold first joint meeting on data center rules as towns weigh power, water and noise impacts.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're starting in Branch County, where Coldwater officials are holding their first joint meeting on data center zoning and regulation.
That sounds like a big one for folks watching how these projects get handled across southern Michigan.
Exactly. City Council, the Planning Commission and the Board of Public Utilities are meeting tonight for an informational session, even though no proposals are active in the area right now.
Why hold the meeting if nothing's on the table yet?
They're getting ahead of it. Utilities and developers are eyeing sites across southern Michigan, and towns want rules in place before anything moves forward.
What kinds of rules are they likely talking about?
Things like zoning limits, noise standards, and how much power and water a project could pull. The goal is to protect residents from sudden spikes in utility bills or other strains.
Residents 30 miles away could feel it too, right?

That's the concern. Data centers drive big load growth, and changes in how utilities recover costs for new lines and substations could mean higher monthly bills for ratepayers across the Lower Peninsula.
We've seen similar pushback elsewhere. Take Wixom yesterday — they advanced new regulations after a 4-3 vote during their moratorium.
Right. That 600,000-square-foot project on 54 acres had residents worried about power demand, water use and noise that could raise household bills.
And Kalamazoo is voting tonight on a year-long pause for all new proposals while they study the limits.
Commissioners there want time to line up new generation so residents avoid sudden utility spikes, plus they've heard complaints about noise and truck traffic from other Michigan projects.
How does Coldwater's approach compare to those?
It's more preparatory. No active fight yet, but they're looking at the same issues: power use, noise, and local impacts before anything lands.
What about the University of Michigan's $1.2 billion site in Ypsilanti? That locked in today over township objections.
Local officials there say they'll keep fighting. Residents farther out could see higher power rates and water strain if the campus moves ahead.
That's a massive project. How does something like that affect the grid overall?

Data centers are a major driver of projected load growth. The state utility regulator is already looking at changing how utilities recover costs for new infrastructure, which could pass more expenses to ratepayers.
And water use is another piece, especially in areas with farmland or limited supply.
Towns are watching that closely. Cooling these facilities takes a lot of water, and communities want protections so it doesn't strain local resources or raise costs.
We've also got Mason resuming debate on a nearby proposal and noise ordinance amendments.
Yes, their city council meets Monday on the Vevay Township hyperscale facility and potential changes to the citizen-initiated noise rules.
And in Marshall, charges were dropped after threats tied to their data center fight.
Calhoun County officials decided no one will face charges over those threats made during heated debates. The city council is still weighing tax breaks and power upgrades.
That tension shows how heated these discussions can get.
It does. Residents worry about rising bills and industrial noise, while officials balance economic development with those concerns.
Branch County has two governments hashing out rules today as well.
That's the joint session in Coldwater we're leading with, but similar talks are happening in other spots like Caledonia Township.
What happens if these meetings produce new ordinances?
New rules on power use, noise limits, and utility cost recovery could set precedents for other towns. It might slow some projects or require developers to address community concerns upfront.
Is there any sense of how many places are pausing or tightening rules right now?
Several across southern Michigan are taking steps — moratoriums, zoning changes, joint reviews — all in response to the same core issues of power demand and local impacts.
And the U-M project shows even big institutions aren't immune to pushback.
True. Township officials plan to keep fighting despite the university confirming the Ypsilanti location.
What should listeners watch for out of tonight's Coldwater meeting specifically?
It's informational, so expect presentations on operations, impacts, and possible ordinance ideas. No decisions tonight, but it could shape future rules if proposals emerge.
And how might that affect folks 30 miles away?
Any new standards on power and noise could influence how utilities plan upgrades and how costs get shared, potentially easing or shifting burdens on ratepayers in neighboring areas.
The state regulator's look at rate recovery changes feels connected.
It is. Data centers are pushing load growth, so how those infrastructure costs get recovered matters for bills statewide.
What kind of timeline are we looking at for these regulatory shifts?
The commission is reviewing changes now, with potential approvals that could roll out over the coming months depending on public input and utility filings.
Meanwhile, Wixom's 180-day moratorium is already in motion after yesterday's vote.
That gives them time to refine rules on the proposed project while addressing resident concerns about bills, water and noise.
Could Wixom's approach become a model?
It might. Other towns are watching how they balance growth with protections during the moratorium period.
Kalamazoo's potential year-long pause would be even longer.
Yes, and it directly responds to power, water and traffic issues seen elsewhere.
Back to Coldwater — since nothing's proposed yet, is this mostly about education?
That's the framing: an informational session to get everyone on the same page about impacts and options before any applications arrive.
Smart move if developers are scouting the area.
Exactly. Being prepared can help avoid rushed decisions later.
Any other towns holding similar prep sessions this week?
Caledonia Township's planning commission is discussing a data center ordinance tonight as well.
And Mason is back at it on their noise rules and the Vevay proposal.
Right. Multiple communities are actively sorting through these questions at once.
What about the tax side? Jackson and others are looking at personal property rules.
Those debates affect how much data centers contribute locally versus what ratepayers might cover for power upgrades.
It all ties back to who pays for the infrastructure these facilities need.
That's the core tension playing out from Ypsilanti to Kalamazoo to Coldwater.
How do you see this evolving over the next few weeks?
More joint meetings, possible moratorium votes, and continued regulator review on rates. Towns are trying to get ahead of the curve.
And residents 30 miles out should keep an eye on how costs get allocated.
Absolutely. Changes in one spot can ripple through utility planning for the region.
Let's shift to quick hits. Graham, what's the latest on the U-M Ypsilanti confirmation?
The university locked in the $1.2 billion site today despite township objections, with locals vowing to keep fighting.
And Kalamazoo's moratorium vote is happening tonight too.
Commissioners will decide on that year-long pause to study power and water limits.
Wixom's zoning changes from yesterday could set a precedent.
The 4-3 vote advances noise and utility cost rules during their 180-day moratorium for the big proposed project.
Marshall dropped charges tied to threats in their debate.
No one will face charges, even as the council weighs tax breaks and upgrades for that proposal.
Mason is resuming its debate Monday.
On the Vevay Township facility and potential noise ordinance tweaks.
Now for on deck. Graham, what meetings can listeners attend tonight?
Mason City Council is reviewing data center zoning and noise rules.
Coldwater has that joint informational session with council, planning and the utilities board.
Caledonia Township Planning Commission is discussing their data center ordinance.
And Kalamazoo City Commission votes on the temporary moratorium resolution.
Plenty happening across the state tonight.
Anything else on the calendar this week?
Those are the main ones lined up for Monday, with more likely as other towns follow suit.
Thanks for walking through all that, Graham.
Anytime. Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.
Good night.
